name: Nalmefene (Opvee, Zurnai)
summary: Fast opioid antidote used in emergencies to reverse opioid overdose—especially dangerous slowed or stopped breathing. Can trigger abrupt withdrawal in opioid-dependent people, so expect agitation and vomiting once they wake up.
description: Nalmefene is an opioid blocker used for suspected opioid overdose when breathing is slow, irregular, or stopped. It can restore breathing within minutes, and it tends to last longer than naloxone. The tradeoff: if someone is opioid-dependent, it can cause sudden, intense withdrawal (agitation, sweating, vomiting, diarrhea). Even if they wake up, you still need emergency care—overdose can come back, especially with long-acting opioids or when huge doses were taken.
patient_summary: Nalmefene is an opioid antidote for suspected overdose. It can restart normal breathing in minutes and may last longer than naloxone, but it can cause abrupt withdrawal in opioid-dependent people. Always call emergency services and keep monitoring—breathing problems can return.

primary_indications: Known or suspected opioid overdose with respiratory and/or central nervous system (CNS) depression

linked_conditions.context: Used when opioid overdose is suspected—especially when breathing is slow, irregular, or stopped. It’s emergency rescue medication, not a substitute for medical care.
Often provided to people at higher overdose risk (or their family/friends) as part of overdose prevention and response planning.
Nalmefene only works on opioids. If the problem is alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives without opioids, it won’t reverse that.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to nalmefene or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.patient_text: When opioids are the cause of slowed or stopped breathing, nalmefene can rapidly reverse those effects—often within minutes—by blocking opioid receptors. Response depends on the opioid involved, the dose taken, and how quickly rescue medication is given.

pharmacokinetics.onset: IV: 2 to 5 minutes; IM/SUBQ: 5 to 15 minutes; Intranasal: ~2.5 to 5 minutes (range up to hours reported in some data sets)
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Intranasal: ~15 minutes (range ~10 minutes to 3 hours); IM: ~2.3 hours; SUBQ: ~1.5 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: ~11 hours (may be longer with severe kidney disease)
pharmacokinetics.duration: At fully reversing doses: >4 hours; recurrence of respiratory depression can still occur, especially with long-acting opioids
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (primarily glucuronidation to inactive metabolite; trace inactive N-dealkylated metabolite); may undergo enterohepatic recycling

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Nalmefene is an emergency opioid antidote. It’s used when someone might be overdosing on opioids and their breathing and/or consciousness is dangerously suppressed. This is the psychiatry-relevant lane: overdose rescue for opioid exposure, often in the setting of opioid use disorder or high-risk opioid prescribing.
items: {link:condition:opioid-overdose:Opioid overdose}: Suspected opioid exposure with slow, irregular, or absent breathing and/or severe unresponsiveness
{link:condition:opioid-use-disorder:Opioid use disorder harm reduction}: Rescue medication kept on hand for self- or buddy-administration in an overdose emergency
Prolonged or recurrent opioid toxicity: May be considered when there is concern for longer-acting opioids, with continuous observation because breathing problems can return

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This is not a “daily med” experience. It’s an emergency moment. Here’s what people commonly report after nalmefene is given and they start coming back:

quotes: They went from scary-quiet breathing to actually taking real breaths again.
It was like a switch flipped—eyes opened, coughing, then breathing normal.
One minute it felt like we were losing them, then they started breathing again.
They woke up furious and sick—sweating, shaking, throwing up.
It looked like instant misery: nausea, diarrhea, chills, panic energy.
They kept saying, 'I feel horrible,' and tried to leave right away.
items.note: Nalmefene can trigger abrupt opioid withdrawal in people with opioid dependence or opioid use disorder. Withdrawal can be intense and may require medical support.

quotes: They were awake but confused and agitated—like they didn’t know where they were.
A lot of pacing, yelling, or trying to stand up immediately.
It can look like panic, but it’s often withdrawal + adrenaline.
They complained their nose and throat burned.
Instant headache and 'hot flush' feeling after the spray.
Nose discomfort was real—even when it worked.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Nalmefene is designed for emergencies, so speed matters. How fast it works depends on how it’s given—and the opioid involved.
key_points: Intravenous (IV): Works in ~2 to 5 minutes (fastest option when IV access is available)
Intramuscular (IM) / Subcutaneous (SUBQ): Works in ~5 to 15 minutes
Intranasal: Often works in ~2.5 to 5 minutes (but real-world timing can vary)
Duration: At fully reversing doses, effects can last >4 hours, but overdose can still return (especially with long-acting opioids or very high-dose exposures)
Half-life: About 11 hours in adults (can be longer in severe kidney disease)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Nalmefene works when opioids are the problem. It blocks opioid receptors, which can reverse slowed or stopped breathing and severe sedation. But it’s not magic and it’s not “one and done.” If the opioid is long-acting, super potent, or taken in massive amounts, breathing problems can come back even after an initial good response—so ongoing monitoring and emergency care are still required.
sections.clinical_details: Nalmefene has high affinity for opioid receptors and a longer duration of action than naloxone at fully reversing doses, which can be helpful in some overdose patterns. The tradeoff is that longer and stronger blockade can also mean longer and more intense withdrawal symptoms in opioid-dependent patients.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Nalmefene can trigger sudden, severe opioid withdrawal. Even if the person wakes up, overdose can come back—call emergency services and keep monitoring breathing.
other: Airway first: Opioid antagonists should be used alongside a patent airway, ventilatory support, oxygen, and circulatory access when possible.
Withdrawal risk: Nalmefene may precipitate opioid withdrawal syndrome in opioid-dependent patients (agitation, sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, fast heart rate, blood pressure swings).

Cardiovascular instability: Use caution in people with cardiovascular disease or when the patient is on meds with cardiovascular effects; abrupt reversal has been associated with pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, and severe blood pressure changes.
Recurrence is real: Respiratory depression can recur even after an initial response—especially with long-acting opioids (e.g., methadone) or repeated high-dose exposures.
Partial agonists: Reversal may be incomplete for partial opioid agonists (e.g., buprenorphine); larger or repeat doses may be needed, with careful monitoring.
Sound-alike risk: Nalmefene may be confused with nalbuphine—double-check the vial/device before giving.
patient_counseling: If you use nalmefene in the community: call emergency services after the first dose. Do not assume the crisis is over because the person wakes up.
If the person stops responding again: start CPR and give a repeat dose as instructed while waiting for help.
Expect withdrawal: sudden nausea, vomiting, sweating, agitation, and diarrhea can happen fast. This can look like panic or aggression, but it’s often withdrawal.
Keep them safe: if they wake up and breathe normally, place them on their side (recovery position) and stay with them.
Do not give opioids to ‘treat the withdrawal’ outside medical care. Trying to override nalmefene can lead to re-intoxication and death once nalmefene wears off.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: The biggest ‘side effect’ is opioid withdrawal—because that’s what happens when you abruptly block opioids in someone who’s dependent. Intranasal use can also cause nose/throat discomfort, headache, and a flushed/hot feeling.
plain_language_list: Opioid withdrawal symptoms (agitation, sweating, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, chills, fast heart rate, blood pressure changes)
Nasal discomfort or nasal pain (intranasal products)

common.incidence: Variable (depends on opioid dependence and dose)
common.patient_note: This is the big one. If the person is opioid-dependent, nalmefene can cause abrupt withdrawal: agitation, sweating, abdominal pain, diarrhea, feverish feelings, nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, and blood pressure swings. Withdrawal can look intense and may require emergency care, but it’s rarely life-threatening by itself.
Headache is frequently reported after administration, especially with intranasal dosing. In an overdose situation, treat headache as secondary—breathing and monitoring come first.

common.incidence: Common (noted in labeling; more noticeable in some routes)
common.patient_note: People may describe a sudden hot, flushed sensation. This can overlap with the stress response and withdrawal symptoms.
Nausea and vomiting can occur as part of withdrawal. Protect the airway—vomiting plus sedation is a dangerous combination.
Burning, nasal pain, congestion, or throat irritation can happen with intranasal administration. It’s unpleasant, but the priority is reversal of respiratory depression.

serious: Pulmonary edema and cardiovascular instability (rare but reported with abrupt opioid reversal): severe shortness of breath, chest pain, pink frothy sputum, new oxygen requirement. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe agitation, confusion, or aggressive behavior (often withdrawal-driven): may require restraint and medical sedation in an emergency setting.
Arrhythmias or extreme blood pressure changes (more likely with preexisting cardiac disease or interacting cardiovascular meds). MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Recurrent respiratory depression after initial reversal: can happen with long-acting opioids or massive exposures—continuous monitoring is required.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Nalmefene’s ‘interaction’ is the point: it blocks opioids. That’s lifesaving in overdose—and brutal in opioid dependence.

items.with: Opioids (natural or synthetic, including high-potency illicit opioids)
items.risk: Rapid reversal of opioid effects can trigger abrupt withdrawal in opioid-dependent people. Some may try to override the blockade by taking more opioids, which can lead to re-intoxication and death as nalmefene wears off.
items.action: Use only when overdose is suspected and breathing/CNS depression is present. After reversal, seek emergency care and monitor continuously for recurrence of respiratory depression.

items.risk: Reversal of respiratory depression may be incomplete; larger or repeat doses may be required. Withdrawal can still be triggered.
items.action: Do not delay emergency care. Continue ventilation support and follow emergency protocols if response is incomplete.

items.risk: Abrupt reversal plus physiologic stress can worsen blood pressure swings, arrhythmias, or pulmonary edema risk in vulnerable patients.
items.action: Use caution, monitor vitals closely, and treat in a medically supervised setting whenever possible.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Nalmefene is emergency rescue dosing for suspected opioid overdose with respiratory and/or CNS depression. In medical settings, airway and ventilation come first (oxygen, assisted breathing, circulation access). Do not keep giving dose after dose once adequate initial reversal has been achieved—over-treatment increases withdrawal and cardiovascular stress without improving outcomes.

adult.overdose_airway_ventilation_note: In most emergency settings, use opioid antagonists alongside establishment of a patent airway, ventilatory assistance, oxygen administration, and circulatory access when possible.
adult.overdose_iv_im_subq_non_opioid_dependent: IV (preferred), IM, or SUBQ: Initial 0.5 mg. If needed, give 1 mg 2 to 5 minutes later. If no clinical response after a total of 1.5 mg, further nalmefene is unlikely to help. Do not administer additional nalmefene once adequate initial reversal is established.
adult.overdose_iv_im_subq_opioid_dependent: IV (preferred), IM, or SUBQ: Initial 0.1 mg. If no evidence of withdrawal, administer 0.5 mg. If needed, give 1 mg 2 to 5 minutes later. If no clinical response after a total of 1.6 mg, further nalmefene is unlikely to help. Do not administer additional nalmefene once adequate initial reversal is established.
adult.recurrent_respiratory_depression: If the patient had adequate initial reversal but then develops recurrent respiratory depression, additional nalmefene may be given using the same dosing strategy used for initial therapy.
adult.intranasal_opvee: 2.7 mg (1 nasal spray) in 1 nostril as a single dose. May repeat every 2 to 5 minutes as needed in alternating nostrils for continued or recurrent respiratory depression until medical assistance becomes available. Use a new device for each dose.

sections.simple_explanation: Think of nalmefene as an emergency ‘opioid off-switch.’ If it works, breathing improves quickly. If the person is opioid-dependent, withdrawal can hit hard—so the goal is to restore breathing, then get medical help and keep monitoring for relapse of overdose symptoms.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: In overdose, saving the patient’s life comes first. Nalmefene should not be withheld in a clear overdose emergency because of pregnancy or breastfeeding concerns, but it can precipitate withdrawal in both the patient and potentially the fetus.
sections.pregnancy: Human pregnancy outcome data are limited for nalmefene. Based on other opioid antagonists, use can precipitate opioid withdrawal in a pregnant patient and may precipitate withdrawal in the fetus as well. In a life-threatening overdose, administer the antidote when clearly indicated—the risk of untreated hypoxia is immediate and severe.
sections.lactation: It is not known if nalmefene is present in breast milk. In an overdose emergency, treat the emergency first. After stabilization, discuss breastfeeding plans and monitoring with a clinician.
sections.pediatrics: Intranasal nalmefene (Opvee) is indicated for adults and pediatric patients aged 12 years and older for emergency treatment of known or suspected opioid overdose with respiratory and/or CNS depression. Follow product-specific instructions and seek emergency medical care immediately after the first dose.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing. Older adults may have age-related changes in drug distribution that can increase initial concentrations. In practice, the emergency indication drives dosing; monitor closely for blood pressure changes, arrhythmias, and agitation after reversal.
sections.hepatic: No dosage adjustment is necessary per provided dosing guidance. Clearance may be decreased in liver disease, so observe closely for duration and adverse effects after administration.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is necessary per provided dosing guidance. In severe kidney disease, clearance may be reduced and half-life prolonged; in clinical settings, consider slower IV administration over ~60 seconds to minimize hypertension and dizziness, and monitor longer.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Respiratory rate and pattern: watch for recurrent respiratory depression after initial reversal
Oxygenation: pulse oximetry and/or arterial blood gas when available
Heart rate and rhythm: monitor for tachycardia, arrhythmias, and instability after abrupt reversal
Blood pressure: monitor for hypertension or hypotension, especially in patients with cardiac disease
Temperature: fever can occur and withdrawal can look like flu symptoms
Level of consciousness: track responsiveness, agitation, confusion, and ability to protect airway
Vomiting/aspiration risk: protect airway and position patient appropriately (recovery position when breathing normally)
Withdrawal severity: agitation, diaphoresis, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, irritability—may require medical support
Need for repeat dosing: if symptoms return, repeat per dosing instructions while continuing CPR/ventilation support and awaiting emergency care

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Nalmefene comes in rescue-ready forms designed for emergencies. The goal is fast administration when seconds matter.
items: Nasal spray (Opvee): 2.7 mg/0.1 mL single-use device (each device delivers one spray; use a new device for each repeat dose)
Auto-injector (Zurnai): 1.5 mg/0.5 mL single-use auto-injector for IM or SUBQ administration (product availability may vary by year/market)
Injection solution (generic nalmefene): 1 mg/mL (commonly supplied in 2 mL vials), used IV (preferred when access is available), IM, or SUBQ

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Nalmefene is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist. Translation: it sits on opioid receptors and blocks opioids from activating them. That’s why it can reverse opioid-induced sedation and respiratory depression—and also why it can trigger sudden withdrawal in opioid-dependent people.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Nalmefene is not a psychiatric “maintenance medication.” It’s emergency harm-reduction—especially relevant in opioid use disorder care plans. In suspected opioid overdose, priorities are airway + breathing + circulation, rapid administration of an opioid antagonist, and immediate emergency medical care. Even when the person wakes up, observation matters because breathing problems can return, and withdrawal-driven agitation can escalate quickly.

seo.title: Nalmefene (Opvee, Zurnai): Emergency Opioid Overdose Reversal, Dosing, Side Effects
seo.description: Nalmefene (Opvee nasal spray; Zurnai auto-injector) is an opioid antagonist for emergency overdose reversal. Learn how fast it works, dosing (intranasal and injection), withdrawal risk, monitoring, and when to repeat doses.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Nalmefene is an emergency opioid antidote used for known or suspected opioid overdose—especially when someone has dangerously slow, irregular, or absent breathing and/or is severely unresponsive. It blocks opioid receptors to reverse opioid effects.

faqs.q: Is nalmefene the same as naloxone?
faqs.a: They’re in the same family (opioid antagonists), but they’re not identical. Nalmefene tends to last longer at fully reversing doses, which can be useful in some overdose patterns. Both can trigger sudden withdrawal in opioid-dependent people, and both still require emergency medical care after use.

It’s fast. IV dosing can work in about 2 to 5 minutes. IM or subcutaneous dosing often works in about 5 to 15 minutes. Intranasal dosing often works in about 2.5 to 5 minutes, though real-world timing can vary.

At fully reversing doses, effects can last more than 4 hours, and it has an adult half-life around 11 hours. But overdose can still return, especially with long-acting opioids or very high-dose exposures—so observation and emergency care are still necessary even after a good initial response.

Yes. If someone is opioid-dependent, nalmefene can trigger abrupt opioid withdrawal—agitation, sweating, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, chills, fast heart rate, and blood pressure swings. Withdrawal can look intense and can require hospitalization, but it’s rarely life-threatening by itself. The overdose is the life-threatening part.

faqs.q: What should I do after giving Opvee (intranasal nalmefene)?
faqs.a: Call emergency services after the first dose. Support breathing (rescue breaths if trained) and monitor closely. If the person stops responding again, begin CPR and give a repeat dose as directed while waiting for medical help. If they wake up and breathe normally, place them on their side and stay with them.

faqs.q: What if I give nalmefene to someone who isn’t on opioids?
faqs.a: If opioids aren’t involved, nalmefene usually won’t help—and it may cause side effects like headache, dizziness, nausea, or nasal discomfort (with intranasal use). The bigger danger is assuming it ‘fixed’ the problem when the cause is something else. Always seek emergency medical care.

faqs.q: Does nalmefene work on buprenorphine overdoses?
faqs.a: Reversal may be incomplete because buprenorphine is a partial agonist with strong receptor binding. Larger or repeat doses may be needed, but this is still an emergency: prioritize ventilation support and activate emergency medical services.

faqs.q: Can someone overdose again after nalmefene works?
faqs.a: Yes. Respiratory depression can recur even after an initial good response—especially with long-acting opioids (like methadone) or massive exposures. That’s why continuous monitoring and emergency care are required.

In a life-threatening overdose, the antidote should not be withheld because of pregnancy. Data specific to nalmefene are limited, and opioid antagonists can precipitate withdrawal in the pregnant patient (and potentially the fetus), but untreated hypoxia is an immediate severe risk. Treat the emergency and get medical care immediately.
